title: Marrow Creek Rising
premise: Theo Villalobos, a pest controller who photographs everything as a private ritual of control, is called to the Marrow Creek farmhouse where something leaves fingerprints at shoulder height on every doorframe. When her own archive reveals an extra chair in every photo taken inside grandma's house, Theo realizes the thing has been following her family for fifty years, waiting for the inheritance papers to be signed. The entity is tied to what her grandfather took from the creek's drowned homestead in 1974, and it will not rest until the theft is returned. Theo must choose between protecting her dying grandmother's legacy and giving back the deed, the locket, and the truth—ending with her wading into Marrow Creek at dawn to return what was taken, trading her invisibility for survival and a home that finally belongs to no one's ghosts.
about_author: Oscar Amberdale is the pen name of a former rural insurance adjuster who spent eleven years documenting other people's worst days before turning to fiction. They write horror about paperwork, property lines, and the things that refuse to stay off the record.

chapters.title: Shoulder Height
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Called to the Marrow Creek farmhouse for a 'rodent problem,' Theo finds greasy fingerprints on every doorframe, all exactly five feet six inches from the floor. She documents everything out of habit, telling herself it's just procedure. The beat is professional unease curdling into personal dread when she recognizes the height: it matches her own.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Reviewing three years of photos from grandma Rosa's house that night, Theo discovers a wooden chair in the corner of every interior shot—a chair she has never seen in person. It appears in photos from 2021 onward. She tells herself it's lens flare, dust, error. The beat is denial dressed up as methodology.

chapters.title: Grandma's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Visiting Rosa, Theo finds a locked ledger box labeled 1974 among the estate papers being prepared for signing. Rosa, sharp but evasive, says some inheritances are debts wearing nice clothes. Theo photographs the box; in the photo, the extra chair sits beside Rosa's bed. The beat is love complicated by suspicion.

chapters.title: What the Deed Says
chapters.summary: POV Theo. At the county records office, Theo pulls the chain of title: the Villalobos farm was purchased in 1974 from the Halloway estate, sold by a woman who drowned in Marrow Creek weeks later. The seller's signature trails off the page mid-letter. The beat is the cold thrill of research becoming the chill of implication.

chapters.title: Fingerprints, Documented
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Back at the farmhouse job, Theo dusts the prints herself and lifts a partial. Her supervisor laughs it off—kids, probably—but the ridge detail is wrong: whorls that spiral inward without end. She files the lift card in her personal archive instead of the company system. The beat is complicity beginning quietly.

chapters.title: The Locket in the Wall
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Chasing a scratching sound inside grandma's wall cavity, Theo cuts through drywall and finds a silver locket engraved E.H., 1973, wrapped in a page torn from the missing ledger. That night's photos show the chair moved two feet closer to Rosa's bed. The beat is discovery shadowed by escalation.

chapters.title: Rosa Remembers Water
chapters.summary: POV Rosa (interleaved with Theo). In a fevered night, Rosa recounts 1974: her husband Amado bought the farm cheap after Edith Halloway's drowning, and Amado came home from the creek with mud to the elbow and wouldn't say what he carried. The beat is grief surfacing as confession half-swallowed.

chapters.title: The Chair Sits Down
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Theo stakes out grandma's house overnight with a camera running. At 3:11 a.m., the footage shows the chair scraping itself to the bedside, facing Rosa, for four hours. Nothing else moves. Theo deletes nothing this time; documentation has become prayer. The beat is terror transfigured into devotion.

chapters.title: Papers Pending
chapters.summary: POV Theo. The estate lawyer, Ms. Okonkwo, pushes to finalize the transfer before Rosa's decline worsens. Theo stalls, lying about a missing signature. Every document she touches now comes back from the copier with faint handprints along the margins. The beat is duty versus dread, both wearing suits.

chapters.title: Descendant of the Drowned
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Tracking the Halloway line, Theo finds a living descendant: Ruth Halloway-Price, sixty, living two towns over, who has spent decades petitioning to reopen the estate. Ruth confirms Edith's locket and a sealed deed addendum vanished in 1974. The beat is alliance offered across old wounds.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV Ruth. Ruth explains the family lore: Edith signed the farm away under pressure the week she died, and the creek keeps its own registry. Whatever Amado pulled from the water must go back before the last Villalobos signs, or the debt transfers whole. The beat is myth delivered as legal instruction.

chapters.title: The Ledger Box Opens
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Theo convinces Rosa to open the box: inside are the deed addendum, Edith's letters, and Amado's confession, unsigned. Rosa admits she's known for fifty years and kept the papers to protect the family's only asset. The beat is inheritance revealed as a wound passed down like jewelry.

chapters.title: Chair Count
chapters.summary: POV Theo. The chairs multiply: one in every archived photo becomes two, then three, arranged in a growing audience around every room Theo has ever photographed, including her own apartment. The entity isn't haunting grandma's house—it's attending Theo's entire documented life. The beat is the collapse of safe distance.

chapters.title: Okonkwo's Deadline
chapters.summary: POV Theo. The lawyer serves notice: signing happens Friday or probate takes the decision from everyone. Theo realizes the entity has been patient precisely because the law is slow—it wants the signature, the seal, the state's blessing on stolen ground. The beat is understanding the enemy's true instrument: paperwork.

chapters.title: Amado's Confession, Unsigned
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Reading Amado's account, Theo learns he didn't steal from Edith—he pulled her body from the creek and kept the locket and addendum as 'evidence,' too frightened to return them, and his silence drowned the truth deeper than the creek did. The beat is pity arriving for the man whose fear caused everything.

chapters.title: Rosa Signs Nothing
chapters.summary: POV Rosa. Lucid for one morning, Rosa refuses to sign, telling Theo: 'I kept the debt so you'd be the one strong enough to pay it.' She gives Theo the box freely. By evening she slips again, and the chair sits closer than ever. The beat is a mother's terrible gift disguised as a burden.

chapters.title: The Company Man
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Theo's employer, pressured by the buyer's agent, orders her to finish the farmhouse job and stop 'spooking' clients. She quits on the spot, leaving her uniform folded on the seat of a chair that wasn't there when she arrived. The beat is liberation that feels like falling.

chapters.title: Friday, Before Signing
chapters.summary: POV Theo. With Ruth as witness, Theo drafts a formal reconveyance: the addendum restored, the locket returned, the fraud acknowledged in writing. Okonkwo, confronted with Amado's unsigned confession, agrees to halt the transfer. But the fingerprints now cover the office windows, shoulder height, dozens deep. The beat is justice assembled from paper while the walls close in.

chapters.title: Marrow Creek, Rising
chapters.summary: POV Theo. The creek floods its banks the night before the filing, swallowing the road to the courthouse. Theo understands: the registry isn't the county's. She packs the locket, the addendum, and the confession, and drives as far as water allows, then walks. The beat is resolve against rising dark.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Waist-deep at the drowned homestead's foundation stones, Theo returns each item—locket to the water, addendum weighted beneath, reading Amado's confession aloud until the current takes the pages. The chairs stand in the shallows around her, facing her, patient. She speaks Edith's name and her grandfather's apology. The beat is restitution as ritual, terror made holy.

chapters.title: The Last Signature
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Dawn. The filing goes through—not a transfer of ownership but a quiet correction restoring the land to the Halloway line, with Rosa's blessing witnessed. The fingerprints stop appearing. The final photograph Theo takes of grandma's room shows no chair at all, just sunlight and an empty corner. The beat is release, and the strange grief of being seen for the first time.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: POV Theo, epilogue. Months later, Theo visits Ruth on the restored land and begins photographing the creek—not to control it, but to honor it. Her archive ends with a single new image: one chair, placed at her own kitchen table, set for a guest who never comes, welcome if they do. The beat is peace earned, vigilance kept, inheritance transformed into stewardship.
